points.label: What overfitting is
points.description: The learner states that overfitting means the model fits the training data too closely — including its noise and quirks — so it performs well on training examples but poorly on new, unseen data.

points.label: How to detect it
points.description: The learner explains that overfitting is detected by comparing performance on training data versus held-out validation/test data: a large gap (low training error, much higher validation error) is the signature of overfitting.

points.label: Causes and remedies
points.description: The learner names at least one cause (model too complex for the amount of data, training too long, too little data) and at least one remedy (more/better data, a simpler model, regularization, early stopping).

misconceptions.summary: The better a model scores on its training data, the better it will be in the real world.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that training performance alone is misleading because the model may have memorized the training set; real-world quality is estimated on data the model never trained on, and chasing training accuracy past a point actively hurts generalization.

misconceptions.summary: Overfitting only happens with huge neural networks, so small models are safe.
misconceptions.correction: The learner clarifies that overfitting is about the balance between model flexibility and data: even a small model (e.g. a high-degree polynomial on ten points, or a deep decision tree on little data) overfits when its capacity is large relative to the available data.

beginner: How can a model be 'too good' at the training data? Isn't fitting the data the whole point?
What does overfitting look like in practice — what numbers would tell me it's happening?
confident: My model gets 100% on the training set, so it has fully learned the problem and will ace new data too.
Overfitting can't happen to me because I'm using a simple model, and simple models never overfit.
skeptic: Modern giant networks have far more parameters than training examples, yet they generalize. Doesn't that break the whole overfitting story?
Where exactly is the line between learning a fine-grained real pattern and fitting noise? Isn't 'noise' just pattern we haven't explained yet?
